title: The Mole Concept, Part A
subtitle: What a mole is, and the formula that links it to particles
lessonIntent: Students can explain what a mole is, why the number 6.022 × 10²³ was chosen, and how N, n, and Avogadro's number relate.
examSkill: Identify whether a question asks for N or n; recognise the formula N = n × Nₐ.
productionNotes: Part A of a 2-part split. Covers the conceptual half of L1, hook, definition, scale, carbon-12 origin, N vs n distinction, and the formula. Part B covers worked examples + practice. Bridge scene at the end teases Part B.
subject: Chemistry
syllabusDotPoints: explore the concept of the mole and relate this to Avogadro's constant to describe, calculate and manipulate numbers of particles, chemical amounts and masses

scenes.caption: The Mole Concept, Part A (Year 11 Chemistry, Module 2)

scenes.heading: How do chemists count atoms they cannot see?
scenes.body: How do you count atoms when you cannot see or weigh one atom?
scenes.caption: The mole lets chemists count invisible particles using a measurable amount.

voiceover.text: OK, here's a question that sounds impossible at first. How do chemists count atoms — when a single atom is way too small to ever see? The answer's actually beautifully simple. It's a counting unit called the mole. By the end of this lesson, you'll be using it like second nature.

scenes.recapSeed: The mole is a counting shortcut for atoms.

scenes.heading: Atoms are impossibly small
scenes.body: Atoms are too small to weigh individually, so chemists count them in huge groups instead.

bullets.text: A single carbon atom weighs ~2 × 10⁻²³ g, too small for any lab balance.
Chemists count atoms in groups, like a dozen, but vastly bigger.
That scale bridges the atomic world to anything we can weigh.

scenes.secondary: Reactions need exact ratios, 2 H per O for water, so chemists needed a counting bridge.
scenes.callout: This is the problem the mole solves.
scenes.caption: Atoms are too small to count individually, chemists needed a counting bridge.

voiceover.text: Let's start by appreciating just how small atoms are. A single carbon atom weighs about two times ten to the minus twenty-three grams. That's so tiny no lab balance on Earth could ever measure it. So chemists do what bakers do — they count in groups. A dozen eggs gets you twelve. A mole of atoms gets you six-point-zero-two-two times ten to the twenty-three. Same idea, just on a totally different scale. And it's that scale that bridges the atomic world to anything you can actually weigh out in the lab.

scenes.recapSeed: Atoms are too small to weigh, count them in groups.

scenes.heading: One mole = 6.022 × 10²³ particles
scenes.body: One mole is the amount of substance containing exactly 6.02214076 × 10²³ elementary entities.
scenes.secondary: Those entities can be atoms, molecules, ions, or formula units, whatever you are counting.
scenes.caption: One mole contains exactly 6.02214076 × 10²³ particles, this is Avogadro's number.

voiceover.text: Alright, here's the actual definition you need to lock in. One mole is the amount of substance containing approximately six-point-zero-two-two times ten to the twenty-three particles. Those particles can be anything you're counting. Atoms, if you're dealing with an element. Molecules, if it's a compound. Or ions and formula units, depending on the substance. The number itself has a name: Avogadro's number. And its symbol is capital N with a little A subscript. You'll see that symbol everywhere in this module, so get comfortable with it now.

scenes.confidenceCheck: Describe the mole as a counting unit for elementary entities.

scenes.heading: How big is 6.022 × 10²³?
scenes.body: The mole is a very large counting unit. Specify the entities being counted.
scenes.callout: A large count bridges particles and measurable quantities.
scenes.caption: A large count bridges particles and measurable quantities.

voiceover.text: How big is 6.022 × 10²³? The mole is a very large counting unit. Specify the entities being counted. 1 mol contains exactly 6.02214076 × 10²³ specified entities. Use rounded 6.022 × 10²³ in these school calculations. A dozen counts 12; a mole counts Nₐ entities.

bullets.text: Use rounded 6.022 × 10²³ in these school calculations.
A dozen counts 12; a mole counts Nₐ entities.

scenes.heading: The current SI definition
scenes.body: One mole contains exactly 6.02214076 × 10²³ specified entities.
scenes.secondary: This links atomic mass to real mass: molar mass in g/mol equals relative atomic mass from the periodic table.
scenes.callout: This is why the periodic table is useful.
scenes.caption: Distinguish the current mole definition from the carbon-12 mass reference.

voiceover.text: Historically, the mole was defined using the number of atoms in twelve grams of carbon twelve. Since twenty nineteen, the SI definition fixes the count directly: one mole contains exactly six point zero two two one four zero seven six times ten to the twenty three specified entities. For school calculations, six point zero two two times ten to the twenty three is a rounded value. Specify what is counted: atoms, molecules, ions or formula units. Carbon twelve remains the reference for relative atomic mass, but is no longer the definition of the mole.

scenes.recapSeed: 1 mole of carbon-12 weighs exactly 12 g.
scenes.confidenceCheck: Relate the mole to Avogadro's constant via the carbon-12 standard.

bullets.text: Current SI definition fixes the particle count directly.
School calculations commonly round Nₐ to 6.022 × 10²³ mol⁻¹.
The 12 g carbon-12 definition is historical.

scenes.heading: N and n are not the same
scenes.body: Wrong instinct: Capital N and lowercase n are interchangeable, both tell you how much you have. Corrected rule: Capital N is the raw count of particles, a huge number with no units. Lowercase n is the amount in moles, a countable quantity with units. They are related by N = n × N_A, but they are not the same thing. In HSC questions, read carefully: does the question ask for N (number of particles) or n (amount in moles)?
scenes.secondary: Lowercase n is the amount in moles, a small number. n = 2 mol → N = 1.204 × 10²⁴ particles.
scenes.callout: Ask first: am I finding N or n?
scenes.caption: N (particles) and n (moles) are completely different, never swap them.

voiceover.text: Here's a trap that catches half the class on their first mole question. Students assume capital N and lowercase n are the same thing — both just 'how much you have'. They're not. Capital N is the raw count of particles — a huge number, no units. Lowercase n is the amount in moles. They're linked by N equals n times Avogadro's number, but they're completely different quantities. So before you do anything on any HSC question, read carefully. Does it want capital N, or lowercase n? Get that wrong, and the whole answer's wrong.

scenes.recapSeed: Capital N counts particles. Lowercase n counts moles.
scenes.confidenceCheck: Distinguish chemical amount (n) from number of particles (N).

scenes.heading: N = n × Nₐ
scenes.secondary: N = particles (no units) · n = moles (mol) · Nₐ = 6.022 × 10²³ mol⁻¹. Units cancel: mol × mol⁻¹ = dimensionless count.

unitCancel.result: N is a particle count, so no mol unit remains.

scenes.caption: N = n × Nₐ connects particle count, moles, and Avogadro's number.

voiceover.text: OK, this is the formula that ties the whole module together. N equals n times Avogadro's number. There are three quantities here. Capital N — that's the number of particles, a raw count. Lowercase n — that's the amount in moles. And Avogadro's number is the bridge between them. The trick: know any two of these, and you can find the third just by rearranging. And notice the units. Moles times moles to the minus one gives you a pure number. That's why N has no units on its answer — it's just a count.

scenes.recapSeed: N = n × Nₐ. Rearrange to find any of the three.
scenes.confidenceCheck: Apply N = n × Nₐ to calculate particles from a chemical amount.
